findings.title: Per-force timing is deferred, but the slice plan assigns "force totals per force" to slice 141
findings.description: Plan entry 141 specifies the harness produces "per-tick timings broken down by phase (spatial build, spatial query, CSR assembly, **force totals per force**, integration)." The design ships `force_total` as one number and defers per-force resolution to slice 142. The extension point is well-designed and the rationale coherent, but this is plan-assigned scope being deferred: 142's own benchmark ("Quadrants cohesion against Numba and NumPy") is meaningless without per-force resolution, so 142 must first extend the harness — churn the harness exists to prevent. Either pull minimal per-force timing into 141 (the tick body already iterates forces; bracketing each call is ~2 lines) or amend the plan entry.

findings.title: Numba backend work is misattributed to slice 144, which per the plan is Quadrants Force Kernels
findings.description: The design states "Slice 144 registers `numba` … delegates to `engine.forces_jit` via the engine's existing JIT-config flag" (also lines 92 and 589). Per the slice plan, 144 is *Quadrants Force Kernels* (porting all `BulkForce` to `@ti.kernel`); no slice in plan 140 owns a Numba benchmark backend. Meanwhile Numba is already delivered (slice 118: `forces_jit.py` and `_jit_config.USE_JIT_KERNELS` exist, default `True`) — meaning the Numba backend is available *now* and per the plan's "Numba and Quadrants slot in as those backends become available" belongs in 141 itself as a near-free second registry row. Correct the attribution and decide who actually registers it.

findings.title: The "numpy" backend's measurement boundary vs. JIT dispatch is unspecified — the baseline label is ambiguous
findings.description: The engine's `BulkForce` wrappers dispatch to Numba `@njit` kernels by default (`USE_JIT_KERNELS = True` in `_jit_config.py`). The design's single registered backend calls the production `tick()` and never states whether it pins the JIT flag off (pure-NumPy forces) or inherits the default — so a row labeled `numpy` would actually measure Numba-compiled force kernels. The plan explicitly requires comparable *NumPy vs. Numba* timings, and slice 142 benchmarks against both; an ambiguous baseline corrupts the comparison this harness exists to make. Specify the flag policy per backend (and consider registering `numpy`/`numba` as two rows in this slice — nearly free).

findings.title: Workload resolution mechanism misdescribes the engine; the "five BulkForce implementations" census omits PropulsionForce
findings.description: Verified against the codebase: `migratory.engine.profile` contains only the `BehavioralProfile` dataclass — no presets or constructors (line 371's "resolve against migratory.engine.profile presets" and 392–394's "constructors used in config/default.yaml" describe nothing that exists; `config/default.yaml` defines a single profile named `default`, not `flocker`/`leader`); no module-level force singletons exist (e.g., `flocking.cohesion_force` — no hits). The engine also ships six weight-driven `BulkForce` implementations plus interaction/repulsor forces, and `config/default.yaml` engages `propulsion_weight: 0.1`, so PropulsionForce is active in the default config — yet lines 138/543 count "five" and the `mid-flock` workload (lines 353–355, claimed "roughly equivalent to the live-server default config formation state") omits propulsion. Consequence: the loader must invent bench-local registries (duplicating config values with drift risk), and the flagship workload is not what the doc claims it is. Describe resolution as bench-local registries honestly, add propulsion to the census and `mid-flock`, and note the profile values are copied from `default.yaml`.

findings.title: The canonical workload schema example is 3-D, but the engine is DIMS=2 — the example cannot load as written
findings.description: The schema example specifies `world_size: [200.0, 200.0, 200.0]` and 3-coordinate `cluster_centers`. The engine is 2-D (`DIMS = 2` in `src/migratory/__init__.py`), and the loader rejects any other arity. The design's primary worked example contradicts the engine it integrates with (consistent with the dimensionality/force-set mismatches behind `mid-flock`'s "equivalent to the live-server default" claim). Fix the example to 2-D.

findings.title: Parity hash capture point is defined two contradictory ways
findings.description: The Scope bullet defines the hash as "SHA-256 of the **post-warmup** `TickResult.positions` and `TickResult.velocities`"; the Parity hash section (lines 458–461) defines it "after the **measure phase**." Those are different states (60 vs. 660 ticks) and different hashes. The parity hash is a consumed interface — slice 145 uses it as the golden reference and a determinism success criterion depends on it — so pick one capture point and state it once.

findings.title: Failure-mode enumeration misses the git-rev-parse, report-write, and batch-mode paths
findings.description: The enumerated failures (missing YAML field, unregistered backend, setup exception with try/finally, TPS < 1) cover the main paths well. Not covered: `git rev-parse HEAD` failing (the git_sha is a schema field, and the harness could run outside a repo), result-file write failures, and `--workload-dir` partial-failure semantics (abort vs. skip-and-continue). Low stakes given the tiny local I/O surface, but the section should name a strategy for each I/O path it introduces.

findings.title: Minor factual wobbles relative to slice 140
findings.description: Line 109–110 quotes slice 140's pytest-benchmark threshold as "`from_numpy_state` < 50 µs"; slice 140's design specifies "< 0.01 ms" (10 µs) at N=3,500. Also line 122's rationale for stub-backend tests "reusing" pytest-benchmark is unclear — deterministic tests over synthetic timings don't need benchmarking machinery. Both are one-line corrections.
